title: Does adoption spread through village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed?
summary: Research programme on the 43 Karnataka village networks of Banerjee, Chandrasekhar, Duflo and Jackson (2013; CC0 replication data, 9,126 households, 44,367 ties): can cross-sectional adoption data tell a simple contagion from a complex one, and which seeding rule stays near the best under every model the data cannot reject? Milestone 1 ports the authors’ estimation code (information model, five moments, identity weights, their 31 × 39 grid, Bayesian bootstrap). It reproduces the data (non-leader take-up 18.7% vs 18.5% published, leaders 24.7% vs 24.8%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98.4% of 1,000 bootstrap draws) and the counterfactual (take-up falls by 0.337 with non-adopters silent; paper 0.32), but not the published point: the minimum is q<sub>N</sub> = 0.05, q<sub>P</sub> = 0.30 for three seeds against 0.10, 0.50, which scores 11 times our minimum; q<sub>P</sub> is weakly identified (95% interval 0.15–1.0) and moves to 0.15–0.25 with two-step weights or quarterly periods. Milestone 2 fits two complex-contagion models on the same information spread, a reinforcement model (logit gains γ per adopting neighbour) and a fractional threshold, and compares them leaving one village out. Both fit better in sample (reinforcement γ = 0.10, positive in 99.5% of 1,000 bootstrap draws, criterion 41% lower; this fine-grid, free-intercept fit is post hoc, the pre-registered coarse grid gave γ = 0) yet predict held-out villages worse than the simple model (better in 13 and 19 of 43; in 12% and 24% of paired bootstrap draws). Take-up by adopting neighbours, 8.3% with none to 35.0% with four or more, is more convex than the simple model's 8.1% to 27.2%, a shape reinforcement, homophily or degree could each leave. Identification and seeding come next.
lede: research programme: does adoption spread through real village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed? On the 43 Banerjee et al. (2013) microfinance villages, reinforcement and threshold models fit better in sample but predict held-out villages worse than the simple information model (better in 13 and 19 of 43), while take-up rises more steeply with adopting neighbours (8% to 35%) than the simple model allows.
